brief.question: What were the main debates in the Australian parliament in 2014, and what positions did members and parties take? Debates that year included The budget fight, The GP co-payment, Data retention and Uni fee deregulation.
brief.answer:
The 2014 parliamentary year was dominated by the government's first budget, delivered in May, and the fierce opposition it provoked. Government speakers, such as the member for Eden-Monaro, defended the budget as a "watershed" necessary to repair what they called Labor's "debt and deficit disaster," citing figures of $667 billion in gross debt and interest payments of $1 billion a month. They argued that tough decisions were needed to avoid worse ones later, and that health and education funding would continue to increase each year. In contrast, Labor members condemned the budget as unfair and a breach of election promises, with the member for Canberra reporting that constituents found it "devastating" and that it unfairly targeted young people, pensioners, and the sick. A censure motion against the Prime Minister over the budget's "broken promises" and new taxes was carried 86 votes to 51.

The most contentious single issue was the proposed $7 GP co-payment, part of the budget's health changes. Labor, led by members like the member for Scullin, who tabled petitions with 9,065 signatures against the measure, argued it was a "GP tax" that would destroy Medicare and universal health care, citing doctors reporting a 30 per cent drop in patient attendance and warnings from the AMA and other health bodies. The government, including the Prime Minister and the member for Bennelong, defended the co-payment as a "modest contribution" to make Medicare sustainable, pointing to a safety net for concession cardholders and children under 16 after 10 visits, and noting that Labor had introduced similar co-payments in the past. Labor's senators announced they would vote against the co-payment, and the opposition moved amendments to condemn the "attack on universal health care."

University fee deregulation was also a major debate, with the House voting against a censure motion opposing the policy by 81 votes to 54. Government members argued deregulation would expand opportunities, including support for 80,000 more students in diploma courses by 2018, while opponents, including Labor, framed it as part of the budget's broader cuts to education and a broken promise. The budget debate also encompassed changes to pensions, foreign aid, and infrastructure spending, with the government arguing these were necessary for fiscal repair and Labor countering that they were unfair and would harm the most vulnerable.
